title: Milestone: A Planet Always Changing
objective: After this level you can connect rocks, moving plates, erosion, deep time and the air into one picture of a planet that never sits still.
summary: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old: slow changes like creeping plates and weathered grains add up over deep time, while the air links rock, water and life on a faster clock.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Nothing on this planet sits still.
cards.body: You started with crystals and grains of sand and climbed all the way to the top of the sky. Now put the pieces into one picture: a planet about 4.54 billion years old whose rock, air and water are always changing, some of it fast and some of it unimaginably slowly.

cards.headline: Slow, but never still
cards.body: You met plate tectonics in World Geography. The plates creep 2 to 15 cm a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. That sounds like nothing, but even at 2 cm a year a plate travels 20 km in a million years, and Earth has had about 4.54 billion years. Rock changes the same patient way: remember Level 10's quartz grain, from granite to sand to sandstone to quartzite?
cards.callout: Slow + deep time = a remade planet

cards.headline: Fast, and felt everywhere
cards.body: The air runs on a faster clock, and it never works alone. Earth's spin bends the wind into spinning storms (Level 49). One big eruption can put sulfur high in the sky and cool the whole planet for one to three years (Level 1). Rock, air, water and life keep trading energy and matter, which is why this course treats them as one system.

mascot.line: It connects: every level so far is one piece of the same machine. Rock, air and water are always passing change along.

cards.headline: Milestone: planet in motion
learned: How moving plates, weathering and deep time keep remaking a planet that never sits still.
Why a rock's crystals and grains show how it formed, and why tough quartz ends up as sand.
Why subduction volcanoes explode, and why young mountains tower while old ones wear low.
How meteorites date the Earth, and how ozone and albedo shape the air and its temperature.

questions.prompt: A plate moving 2 cm a year travels _____ in a million years.

options.label: about 2 m
about 200 m
about 20 km
about 2,000 km
options.rationale: That's a hundred times too far.

questions.explanation: 2 cm a year for a million years is 2 million cm, or 20 km.

questions.prompt: Put the quartz grain's path through the rock families in order.
questions.explanation: The quartz grain goes from granite to sand to sandstone to quartzite.

questions.prompt: Why can Cascade volcanoes like Mount St. Helens erupt explosively while Hawaii's lava mostly flows out quietly?

options.label: Cascade volcanoes sit much closer to the Equator
options.rationale: Latitude doesn't set how a volcano erupts.

options.label: Hawaii's volcanoes are too young to explode
options.rationale: The difference is the magma, not the age.

options.label: Cascade magma is runny basalt that gushes out
options.rationale: Runny basalt is Hawaii's; it lets gas escape.

options.label: Their high-silica magma is sticky and traps gas

questions.explanation: More silica makes magma thick and sticky, so gas stays trapped until it bursts out. Subduction feeds the Cascades that kind of magma.

questions.prompt: Why are the Himalayas still towering while the Appalachians, perhaps once as high, are now much lower?

options.label: The Appalachians sank back beneath the ocean floor over time
options.rationale: They stand on land; erosion wore them down.

options.label: The Himalayas are still rising; the Appalachians stopped long ago
Glaciers have never reached high enough to carve the Himalayan peaks
options.rationale: Ice isn't the difference; ongoing uplift is.

options.label: Himalayan rock is far too hard for erosion to wear down
options.rationale: All rock erodes; uplift keeps pace there.

questions.explanation: India is still pushing into Asia, raising the Himalayas more than 1 cm a year. The Appalachians stopped rising about 300 million years ago and have been eroding ever since.

questions.prompt: Why do scientists date meteorites, not Earth's own rocks, to find Earth's age?

options.label: Earth's rocks are too hard to cut open
options.rationale: Hardness isn't the problem; missing rocks are.

options.label: Meteorites hold far more radioactive material
options.rationale: The same clocks work in both; Earth lacks its first rocks.

options.label: Earth's rocks have no radioactive clocks
options.rationale: Many do: zircons are dated that way.

options.label: Plate tectonics recycled Earth's oldest rocks

questions.explanation: Earth's first rocks were recycled and destroyed, so scientists date meteorites, which formed with the Solar System 4.53 to 4.58 billion years ago.

questions.prompt: Why does the stratosphere warm with height when the air below it cools?

options.label: It is heated by the sunlit ground far below
Its ozone absorbs ultraviolet light as heat
It holds most of the water vapor
Meteors heat it as they burn
options.rationale: Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere.

questions.explanation: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs the Sun's ultraviolet light and turns it into heat.

questions.prompt: Which change would make a patch of Earth absorb more sunlight?

options.label: Fresh snow falling on bare ground
options.rationale: Snow reflects more, so less is absorbed.

options.label: Dark blacktop repaved with lighter concrete
Snow-covered ice melting into open ocean
A dark field covered with bright snow

questions.explanation: Open ocean reflects about 6% of sunlight and snow-covered ice up to 90%, so swapping ice for ocean means far more is absorbed.
